bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Arithmetic and geometric progressions.

## The idea in plain language

Some sequences grow by **adding** the same thing each time: 3, 7, 11, 15 — always plus 4. That is an arithmetic progression, and it is like climbing stairs of equal height.

Others grow by **multiplying**: 3, 6, 12, 24 — always doubling. That is a geometric progression, and it is like a rumour spreading, each round bigger than the last.

Spotting which one you are looking at is most of the work.

## What is actually going on

For an arithmetic progression, check that consecutive differences are constant. For a geometric progression, check that consecutive **ratios** are constant.

The sum of an AP has a lovely shortcut: pair the first term with the last, the second with the second-last, and each pair has the same total. That is why the sum is just the average of the first and last terms, times how many terms there are.

For hybrid or pattern-spotting questions, write out the differences between consecutive terms. If those differences themselves form a recognisable pattern, you have found the rule.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Standard summation formulas

**Spot it when:** the sum of the first n squares, cubes, or integers.

1. $\sum n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\sum n^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$, $\sum n^3 = \left(\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2$.
2. Match the series to the right formula, then substitute.
3. Note the sum of cubes is the square of the sum of integers — a useful check.

**Worked through:** $\sum_{1}^{10} n^2 = \dfrac{10 \times 11 \times 21}{6} = 385$.

### 2. Spotting the pattern in an unfamiliar series

**Spot it when:** a list of numbers with the next term wanted, and no obvious AP or GP.

1. Write the differences between consecutive terms.
2. If those are constant it is an AP; if they themselves form a pattern, look at second differences.
3. Check ratios instead if the terms grow quickly.

**Worked through:** 2, 6, 12, 20, 30 has differences 4, 6, 8, 10, so the next term is $30 + 12 = 42$.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Recall the three standard summation formulas.
- Use differences and ratios to identify an unfamiliar pattern.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of 5, 9, 13, 17, ...
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
The common difference is 4, so this is an AP with $a = 5$ and $d = 4$.

The 20th term is $a + 19d = 5 + 76 = 81$.

Sum $= \dfrac{n}{2}(\text{first} + \text{last}) = \dfrac{20}{2}(5 + 81) = 10 \times 86 = 860$.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Pairing shows why: 5 with 81, 9 with 77, and so on — ten pairs each totalling 86.

workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
The differences are 4, 6, 8, 10 — increasing by 2 each time, so the next difference is 12.

The next term is $30 + 12 = 42$.

(The pattern is $n(n+1)$: $1 \times 2$, $2 \times 3$, $3 \times 4$, and so on.)
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: When a sequence is neither arithmetic nor geometric, the differences are the first place to look.

formulaCards.title: Geometric progression
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $n$th term $= ar^{n-1}$. Sum of $n$ terms $= \dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$ for $r \neq 1$.

formulaCards.title: Infinite geometric sum
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: If $|r| < 1$, the sum to infinity is $\dfrac{a}{1 - r}$.

commonTraps: Using $a + nd$ for the $n$th term. It is $a + (n-1)d$ — the first term has taken no steps yet.
Applying the infinite-sum formula when $|r| \geq 1$, where the series does not converge.
Assuming a sequence is arithmetic after checking only one difference. Check at least two.
